Lots of these words have more than one meaning. If you look them up in a dictionary or online, you will find the other meanings (or you might know them already).

Accept: To agree to receive, e.g. “He accepted the pen as a present.”
Except: Not including, other than, e.g. “I work every day except Saturday.”

Affect: to have an effect on or make a difference to, e.g. “The damp began to affect my health.”
Effect: A change which is the result of an action or other cause, e.g. “The warm weather had a positive effect on my health.”

Ball: A sphere that you play with, e.g. “I threw him the ball.”
Bawl: Cry loudly, e.g. “The baby began to bawl.”

Berry: A kind of small fruit, e.g. “There was a juicy, red berry on the raspberry bush.”
Bury: Cover with soil underground, e.g. “The pirate dug a hole to bury the treasure.”

Brake: What you do to slow down a car or bike (or the thing you use to do that), e.g. “Squeeze the brake to slow done your bike!”
Break: Damage, e.g. “If you drop the box of eggs, they will break.”

Fair: Treating people in an equal way, e.g. “I’ll be fair – you can have five sweets each.”
Fare: What you pay when you get on a bus or train, e.g. “The driver asked for the fare and I paid £3.50.”

Grate: What you do to cheese (or other food) using a grater to make little bits, e.g. “Please can you grate some cheese onto my pasta?”
Great: Another word for amazing, e.g. “You have drawn a great picture of mum!”

Groan: Make a deep inarticulate sound conveying pain or despair, e.g. “Ben groaned and pulled the duvet over his head.”
Grown: Got bigger, e.g. “The sunflower had grown another 6cm!”

Here: The place where you are, e.g. “Here is my shoe!”
Hear: What you do with your ears to sense sound, e.g. “I can hear the phone ringing.”

Heel: The back part of a foot or shoe, e.g. “There is a hole in the heel of my sock.”
Heal: When a hurt gets better, e.g. “I cut my hand but it will heal soon.
He’ll: Short for “he will”, e.g. “I think he’ll come to the shops with me.”

Knot: What you get if you tie string together, e.g. “Tie a knot in the rope to stop the boat floating away.”
Not: This makes something the opposite or negative, e.g. “That is not my cat.”

Mail: Another word for post or letters, e.g. “I got a parcel in the mail!”
Male: The opposite of female, e.g. “A male lion has a mane.”

Main: The most important one, e.g. “The main road runs through the middle of town.”
Mane: The hair on the head of a horse or male lion, e.g. “The horse flicked its mane out of its eyes.”

Meat: Food made from the flesh of an animal, e.g. “Tigers eat meat but sheep do not.”
Meet: Come together, e.g. “Let’s meet outside the coffee shop.”

Medal: Usually a metal disc on a ribbon given as a prize, e.g. “She got a gold medal for winning the race.
Meddle: Interfere in something that is nothing to do with you, e.g. “Do not meddle in other people’s affairs.”

Missed: Didn’t hit or didn’t catch, e.g. “I missed the train.”
Mist: Light fog or low cloud, e.g. “The mist in the valley was cold and grey.”

Peace: Quiet, calm, the opposite of war, e.g. “I enjoyed five minutes peace before the children came home.”
Piece: A bit of something, e.g. “I ate a large piece of chocolate cake.”

Plain: Not decorated, basic, e.g. “I like eating plain food.”
Plane: Short for “aeroplane”, e.g. “I flew in an aeroplane to France.”

Rain: Water that falls from the sky, e.g. “I put up my umbrella to keep off the rain.”
Rein: The strap a rider uses to control a horse, e.g. “I pulled on the rein to stop my horse.”
Reign: The period of time when a king or queen is in charge, e.g. “Queen Victoria’s reign lasted 63 years and seven months.”

Scene: The place where something real or fictional happened, e.g. “First, the author set the scene by describing what the cottage was like.”
Seen: Observed something with your eyes, e.g. “Have you seen my socks?”

Weather: The conditions outside, e.g. “The weather today was cold and snowy.”
Whether: Expresses a choice or an alternative, e.g. “I had to decide whether to put on my coat.”

Whose: a possessive pronoun, like “my” which asks or tells who something belongs to, e.g. “Whose shoes are these?”
Who’s: short for “who is”, e.g. “Who’s going to set the table?”

How to Play:

  1. Player 1 chooses a pair (or trio) of homophones. You can think of your own or roll the die below.
  2. Player 1 says a sentence that includes both words, but instead of saying the words, says “splat”.
  3. Player 2 must guess what the words are.
  4. When Player 2 has guessed, swap over!
  5. Repeat a few times and see what funny sentences you can think of!

The Aim of the Game:

To guess which homophones the other player has used in a sentence.
